items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I always thought he was like as great a jazz writer as Monk

ctx.x: I think that was a trio, my playing on…. I think Strayhorn is some— … his music, I wish I could really digest well. Somehow, his music had a more … different, uh … dimension. I mean, Duke was always a great writer, but his music is more, uh … suited with singing, maybe, to words, and so on. But I think Duke‟s greatness was probably orchestration. [?? Track begins in mid-sentence with syllable ui 憂い, possibly the Japanese term for sad, gloomy], you know, a Japanese, it has a … it‟s a more different dimension; his…

think about certain things, that particular music. It‟s not hunky-dory, happy-happy, or anything like that. It was, of course, his last one, “Blood Count,” it really sounds like a blood count, you know. He‟s one of probably … I always thought he was like as great a jazz writer as Monk, but Strayhorn has … one doesn‟t have to be a jazz musician to appreciate or understand or, you know, the music. For Monk‟s music, you kind of have to be a jazz connoisseur to appreciate his music, I think. But Strayhorn‟s is music…

Well, obviously, as you said, the Strayhorn family saw some, saw your music, your interpretation of Strayhorn as very, very valuable, so that‟s great. You know, when you were talking earlier about John Lewis and how he brought in a lot of, you know, Western classical influence….

items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: They were very open, so I could sit in with Monk’s group if I know the tune, which I did, and things like that.

ctx.x: No. Actually I never thought about it until Duke Ellington died. Before that, you know it was just a Japanese traditional concept, or being Japanese playing jazz was some sort of a handicap. When I was growing up in Japan as a player, they always said that Filipino people have better feeling than Japanese, and indeed the Filipino players played better than us, and it’s simply because they have a longer history. They weren’t under — they were colonized by America so they are more exposed for jazz, much longer than…

butter.” The smell of butter means very American. Because butter is western. Japanese traditionally, we have no butter. So they used to say her playing smells of butter. That’s what they used to say. So that has been going on for a long time. When Duke Ellington died, it was ’73, or ’74 I think, and there was a Village Voice, Nat Hentoff had a memoir. And he was talking about that fact that Duke was, how proud he was about his race. And he was pointing out so many music was based on his race, which I knew some…

community or history that has been pretty good to me. However people always say that, you know I barely played for about thirteen years, and the people always say well you had a terrible time, a difficult time. And I never thought I am having a difficult time. Because everybody else did I thought. When I look back I think those times were very important times. If I didn’t have that I probably didn’t come to that conclusion. I think it’s having sort of like, not a battle, but to become more warm. It’s very…
